turn_text: This is AgriPulse's OpenMic. I'm your host, Jeff Nally. Our guest this week is North Dakota U.S. Senator John Hoban. AgriPulse's OpenMic is brought to you by NCIS, the National Crop Insurance Services. America's Crop Insurance Industry provides individualized protection on more than 290 million acres of farmland. Crop Insurance remains the smartest, most efficient way to secure America's food, fiber, and fuel supply. AgriPulse Openite continues with U.S. Senator John Hovin. Next. America's crop insurance industry is thankful for the continued support of farmers, commodity organizations, rural businesses, lenders and lawmakers who are fighting to maintain a strong farm safety net. The National Crop Insurance Services provide individualized protection on more than 290 million acres of farmland. Crop insurance remains the smartest, most efficient way to secure America's food, fiber, and fuel supply. This is AgriPulse OpenMic. Following an exhaustive hearing on New Farm policy last week in Washington, Senator John Hoban says the farm voice is clear in support of risk management, research, and access to capital at a new farm bill. Surrounding that debate, Hoban says his state and their neighbors are experiencing a severe drought. And while government programs are helping, they're not enough.

Some of the federal programs help. We've done work to get the CRP acres open. We've gotten permission to go out and hay and graze in contiguous counties. Matter of fact, our whole state now is open for that. We're working through ELAP to get, you know, some assistance for hauling hay and getting water for livestock. So we're taking those kind of steps. You've got the livestock forage program as well that provides some payment on a per head basis for livestock, forage, and feed. But the reality is, you know, those things help some, but, you know, really don't offset the effects of a sort of drought like we have.
Are there enough insurance company adjusters that is there enough FSA staff to facilitate the programs that are available for producers there?

Well, we've taken those steps to and we've included efforts both through the Agaprops Committee and working with the Secretary of Agriculture, Sonny Perdue, to get additional people out on the ground, both FSA folks as well as push on crop adjusters so that those ranchers can get into some of those crops that aren't going to make it and cut them or graze them up for feed
senator is there an urgency on the agriculture committee to get sunny produce some help down at the department of agriculture

absolutely uh... you know really trying to put a push on both in terms of getting nominees in the slots and then uh... getting them approved no question we're trying to put a real push behind it and get those slots filled
thoughts on steve sinceky as perhaps the deputy secretary of agriculture at u-s-d-a

Yeah, generally good. I think, you know, I know Sonny Purdue very well. We serve together as a governor, governors for about eight years. And so, you know, he's solid and the team that he's building is solid and going to be very responsive.

Do you have an opinion on Sam Clovis, particularly as an undersecretary for research, education and economics? Ms. Stabenow and some others have raised some flags that a scientist should hold that post.
Well, you know, everybody's going to have their opinion and he'll go through the hearing process, but I think he'll get a favorable reception.
Okay. And the Secretary of Agriculture talking about eliminating an undersecretary for rural development, but adding an undersecretary for trade?

Well, good on adding the undersecretary for trade. As you know, that was in the farm bill. And of course, Secretary Purdue is stepping up and filling that as far as the undersecretary for rural development in our AG Appropriations Committee, we funded that position so we want to see that under Secretary for Rural Development continue as part of an emphasis on the importance of Rural Development.
How important is spending going to be in developing this new farm bill?

Well, it's going to be a challenge, you know, just because of the budgetary pressures here, you know, in Washington and on behalf of our nation. So there's no question it's going to be a funding challenge, but We've got a really strong case to make. In the last Farm Bill, we saved $23 billion. If you score that over 10 years, that's more than $100 billion in savings. And so the RAG has already stepped up and helped in terms of savings as far as the debt and deficit. And we face some real tough time in agriculture now, not only because of low prices and drought, but also some of the challenges with trade. So I think there has to be a recognition You know, that good farm policy benefits every single American every single day because of the highest quality lowest cost food supply in the world. Sports, 16 million jobs. We have a favorable balance of trade. I think when you put those things together, we really have a strong case to make. But, you know, it'll still be a challenge. No doubt.
